title: Measuring the Swarm Economy
gist: Gavin Morrison argues AI capability now scales with the number of coordinating agents ('swarm scaling', lambda≈0.57 per Toby Ord), as shown by OpenAI's 10,000-agent, 88-hour Navier-Stokes proof and the 1,200-agent Hugging Face hacking incident. Single-agent benchmarks are obsolete; the industry needs multi-agent evaluations plus liability, insurance and contract frameworks, because swarm-driven economic gains are bottlenecked on multi-agent alignment and trust.

insights.claim: OpenAI used a swarm of over 10,000 parallel coordinating agents to produce a 'forced blowup' proof of the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem in 88 hours, exchanging 2.7 million messages and using about 130 billion output tokens.
insights.speaker: Gavin Morrison
insights.so_what: Multi-agent swarms convert massive inference compute into frontier results, a new demand driver for tokens and chips.
insights.quote: In the span of 88 hours, a solution was achieved by a set of over ten thousand agents operating in parallel and coordinating their behavior.

insights.claim: Beyond pretraining and test-time inference, a third scaling law has emerged: scaling the number of agents on a task lets huge amounts of compute be spent in exchange for faster results on bigger problems.
insights.speaker: Gavin Morrison
insights.so_what: A new axis of compute consumption supports continued AI infrastructure spending.
insights.quote: It has now been established that scaling the number of agents for a task can enable huge amounts of compute to be expended in return for faster results on bigger problems.
insights.locator: A new “scaling law” has come into play.

insights.claim: Toby Ord, using data from OpenAI's Sol 5.6 launch, found that multiplying agents by N gives the same performance boost as scaling each agent's compute by N^0.57 (the parallelizability exponent lambda), so 16x more agents equals roughly 4.9x more per-agent inference.
insights.speaker: Toby Ord
insights.so_what: Swarm scaling is compute-inefficient, implying disproportionately high token consumption per unit of capability gained.
insights.quote: multiplying the number of agents working on a problem by N gives the same boost to performance as scaling the compute budget for each individual by a factor of N^0.57
